item.title: Who gets to be Italian? The rise and rise of Islamophobia in Italy. [ middleeasteye ]
item.description:
Who gets to be Italian? The rise and rise of Islamophobia in Italy

Submitted by Dalia Ismail on Fri, 09/25/2026 - 13:30
Giorgia Meloni's announcement of a ban on the burqa and niqab in schools comes as the Italian right competes over the demonisation of Muslims
A Muslim takes part in a mass in Santa Maria in Trastevere church in Rome on 31 July 2016 (AFP)
Off

When Giorgia Meloni addressed hundreds of young supporters of her Brothers of Italy party in Rome on Sunday, she chose the school as a way of illustrating who she thought was and was not Italian. 

“It cannot be that, in an Italian classroom, Italian children are the ones who feel cornered because they have become the minority. It cannot happen,” the prime minister told Fenix, the annual festival organised by National Youth, Brothers of Italy’s youth wing. 

On Wednesday, Meloni’s government approved a ban on the burqa and niqab in schools and announced that a 30 percent cap will be imposed on children without Italian citizenship or poor knowledge of the Italian language in the first year of primary, middle and high school. 

Meloni described the measures as “common-sense tools that do not divide but really help to integrate”.

The announcement comes as Italy moves towards an expected national election in 2027, with immigration, Islam and national identity once again central battlegrounds on the political right.

Meloni’s speech and the legislation immediately raised practical questions: who exactly is “foreign” and who is Italian? 

Italy already has guidelines recommending a 30 percent ceiling for pupils without Italian citizenship. The distinction between “Italian” and “foreign” children also rests on citizenship, rather than on where children were born or have grown up. 

Italy's citizenship system is based primarily on descent: children born in the country to non-Italian parents generally do not acquire Italian citizenship automatically. 

As a result, children who were born in Italy and have spent their lives there can still be officially classified as foreign citizens. And Meloni's intervention did not come in isolation.

A mosque in Mestre

Last week, a banner declaring “Your integration is our ruin” appeared outside a school in Mestre, on the mainland opposite Venice, in an area with a large Bangladeshi community. Nearby, at a public park used by Muslims for Friday prayers, “No Islam” and Christian crosses were painted on the ground and on a wooden structure.

The incidents come as a dispute over plans by members of Mestre's Bangladeshi community to build a permanent mosque and Islamic centre on the site of a former sawmill becomes increasingly heated. The community has bought the land, but the project requires approval from local authorities.

'We cannot allow an immigrant to become an Italian citizen so easily because then this citizen votes'

- Roberto Vannacci, Futuro Nazionale

One of the project's most vocal opponents has been Anna Maria Cisint, a European parliament member for the right-wing Lega party who has repeatedly campaigned against the construction of new mosques. 

In February, during a Lega protest outside the proposed site in Mestre, Cisint declared that the mosque would not be built if her political camp remained in power.

On the same Sunday that Meloni announced her school measures, Cisint appeared at the Lega’s annual rally in Pontida, the northern Italian town that has hosted the party's symbolic gathering for decades. 

She was joined on stage by four activists from Nemesis, a French far-right group that describes itself as feminist. The activists were wearing full-face veils. As people on stage and in the crowd chanted “take it off”, the women removed them.

“The threat is radical Islam,” Cisint told the rally. “We will never allow them to Islamise our home. Never.”

The convergence was striking. In Rome, Meloni warned that Italian children could become a minority in classrooms; at Pontida, a coalition politician warned of the country’s “Islamisation”; and in Mestre, a mosque dispute was enflamed by anti-Muslim slogans.

The rogue general

At the same time, another political force is trying to carve out space further to the right.

Roberto Vannacci, a former army general who first became a national figure after publishing a book attacking immigration, feminism and LGBTQ+ rights, entered the European Parliament in 2024 with the Lega. 

The “rogue general” later broke with the party and founded Futuro Nazionale, a new far-right movement that has made “remigration” - the removal of migrants from Italy - one of its defining themes. 

The party is now registering around eight percent in some opinion polls ahead of the next general election, while the Lega, still led by Deputy Prime Minister Matteo Salvini, has fallen below six percent. The figures have intensified a struggle over voters on the Italian right and over how far its politics on immigration and national identity can move.

It was against this backdrop that Vannacci made one of his most explicit statements yet about who should be allowed to become Italian. Speaking at a conference on urban security organised by a police union in Turin on 18 September, he argued that Italy should not make citizenship easier for immigrants.

“We cannot allow an immigrant to become an Italian citizen so easily because then this citizen votes,” Vannacci said. “And when he votes, he does not vote for the good of Italian citizens but for his own good.”

When challenged over whether he was simply worried that naturalised citizens would not vote for him, Vannacci replied: “I'm not afraid that they won't vote for me. I'm afraid that they won't vote for Italy.”

Who gets to be Italian?

The former general’s argument raises a fundamental question: what happens when the person born or raised in Italy actually becomes Italian. 

Fioralba Duma, an Italian-Albanian activist with the campaign group Italians Without Citizenship, told Middle East Eye that Meloni's remarks were particularly troubling because many of the children described as “foreign” have never known another country.

“It is sad, because you realise how little responsibility those in power take when dealing with such important issues, and how little they do to protect children and guarantee them equal opportunities,” she said.

'Petrol is approaching three euros a litre, and she is talking about girls wearing the niqab at school when there are no girls wearing the niqab at school'

- Ahmed Vall, Islamic Community of Rome

“Our struggle started 10 years ago - and for many people even earlier - but instead of reducing the number of people who are foreigners only on paper, that number continues to grow every year. We used to talk about newly arrived migrants. Today we are talking about third generations: the grandchildren of immigrants, born in Italy.”

Duma’s comments point to a contradiction that has become increasingly visible in Italy's political debate. 

Politicians can speak of “foreign pupils” in classrooms even when those pupils were born in Italy, have spent their lives in the Italian education system and may speak Italian as their first language.

Italy's citizenship law remains largely based on jus sanguinis, or citizenship by descent. A referendum in June 2025 sought to reduce from 10 to five years the period of legal residence required for non-EU adults to apply for citizenship. 

Around two-thirds of those who voted backed the proposal, but turnout was only around 30 percent, well below the 50 percent required for the result to be valid.

The Muslim threat narrative 

The controversy over the proposed mosque in Mestre shows how these arguments are playing out beyond the classroom.

Part of the city's large Bangladeshi community wants to turn the site of the former sawmill into a permanent Islamic centre capable of hosting up to 1,500 worshippers. But the project requires a change in the area's planning designation, and Venice's centre-right mayor, Simone Venturini, has opposed the project.

‘Our land is not for sale’: Italian activists challenge Israeli-linked solar projects
Read More »

Muslim organisations, meanwhile, accuse politicians of turning Islam into a political threat by focusing on issues that have little bearing on the everyday reality of Muslims in Italy.

Ahmed Vall, president of the Islamic Community of Rome, described Meloni's announcement on the niqab as “propaganda”. “We have never seen girls going to school wearing the niqab. It is a false problem,” he told MEE.

“Petrol is approaching three euros a litre, and she is talking about girls wearing the niqab at school when there are no girls wearing the niqab at school,” he said.

Vall said his organisation was prepared to challenge discriminatory measures through legal means, pointing to a complaint already filed against Lega MEP Silvia Sardone after she filmed and confronted a woman wearing a niqab in Turin. 

Rula Mohamed, another Islamic Community of Rome activist, described the situation more starkly, telling MEE that Islamophobia in Italy had reached “extreme levels”.

“What we are seeing today is the extreme result of something that has been cultivated for years,” she said. This climate, Mohamed argued, had been built not just by the right wing, but through years of Muslims being portrayed in the media as dangerous and incompatible with Italian society.

This, she said, had been compounded by the failure of much of the centre-left to seriously confront Islamophobia. 

Islamophobia
Milan, Italy

item.title: Eviction drives are not sustainable. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The recent drive by Dhaka South City Corporation (DSCC) to clear hawkers from the key stretch between Paltan and Gulistan once again highlights our all-too-familiar urban dilemma.
While reclaiming footpaths for pedestrian comfort and relieving bottleneck traffic are necessary goals that must not be ignored, the high-handed eviction drives we have been seeing this year can never be a permanent solution. History tells us that once law enforcement officers depart, vendors and hawkers inevitably return.
What must also be recognized is that these individuals are not criminal trespassers but are working citizens that are striving to earn an honest living in an informal economy that supports millions of families.
Driving hawkers away without viable, long-term alternatives therefore fails to address the root issue.
Whether we like it or not, informal street vending has long been a vital pillar of urban livelihoods and provides a service to millions of city dwellers. Having clearances don’t do much to solve urban congestion but instead create a game of cat-and-mouse that ultimately wastes civic administrative resources and destabilizes vulnerable households.
To break this endless cycle, we must move from blanket crackdowns toward structured integration.
The DSCC's proposal to register hawkers and assign designated zones is a step in the right direction, but it must be expanded into a comprehensive, transparent framework.
Having a limited number of hawkers registered is no solution for every other person who depends on the streets to earn a livelihood. At a time when the economic challenges for Bangladesh are greater than ever, there must be a better solution than simply removing vendors from the streets.
Dhaka belongs to all its residents -- pedestrians, commuters, and street vendors alike. We expect the city corporation to balance the public right to accessible footpaths with the human right to a livelihood.
Order on the streets must be a goal, but without jeopardizing the survival of the working class.

item.title: A call for climate action. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
It is certainly commendable that Bangladesh has, once again, used the global stage to make it clear that the climate crisis cannot be addressed through promises alone.
For Bangladesh, a country that contributes less than 0.5% of global greenhouse gas emissions while remaining among the countries most vulnerable to climate impacts, the existential threat of climate change only grows.
To that end, speaking at a high-level meeting on “Climate Action and the Just Transition” at the UN Headquarters in New York during the events of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s call for urgent international action must be heeded.
The points he raised, including deeper emissions cuts, predictable climate finance, access to climate-smart technologies, greater renewable energy investment, and full implementation of the Loss and Damage Fund are salient and important, not just for us, but most of the Global South.
The principle of climate justice is particularly important: Countries that have contributed most to global emissions must recognize their greater responsibility, and ensure that vulnerable countries have the resources and technology needed to adapt.
Of course, Bangladesh must demonstrate that international support will be matched by serious domestic action. The government has outlined plans to plant 250 million trees, restore rivers and canals, expand renewable energy, and promote green industries. It has also allocated nearly $3.19 billion for climate adaptation.
These are substantial commitments, but their value will ultimately depend on transparency, effective implementation, and measurable results.
Bangladesh is absolutely right to demand stronger global action. But international pledges must translate into financing, technology, and tangible resilience on the ground.
The climate crisis is already affecting livelihoods, food security, and economic stability. There is little room left for delay, and both global partners and Bangladesh have a collective responsibility to turn these commitments into action.

item.title: AI titans hit the brakes: What it means for Bangladesh. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Recently, some leading figures in the artificial intelligence (AI) industry, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, have warned that AI capabilities are advancing faster than our ability to make them safe, reliable, and controllable.
This raises three questions:
For years, the same leaders pushed businesses to adopt AI quickly, and it worked. AI has become a mainstream business tool across industries, promoted as a major source of productivity and economic growth.
Until recently, most AI tools functioned as assistants. A user gave the system an instruction, the AI produced an answer, and a human decided what to do with it. The human remained in control.
That is changing. Newer AI systems are becoming more autonomous. Instead of answering a single question, an AI “agent” can be given a broader goal and determine the steps needed to achieve it -- searching for information, using software, writing and running code, and carrying out actions with less human involvement.
This shift, from AI as a tool to AI as an agent, is behind the concern.
The more autonomy a system has, the greater the consequences if it misunderstands an instruction, makes an error, is manipulated, or acts in a way its operator did not intend.
The concern is not that today's AI will suddenly become an independent decision-maker with its own agenda. It is that increasingly capable systems could eventually be given more authority than humans can effectively supervise.
Some researchers also worry about “recursive self-improvement,” in which AI systems help develop more capable systems, potentially advancing faster than researchers can test or control them.
There are also immediate risks. Powerful AI can be misused for cyberattacks and fraud. It does not need malicious intentions to cause harm; it only needs to be a powerful tool in the wrong hands or connected to an important system without adequate safeguards.
Autonomous agents raise the stakes because they can take multiple actions without a person approving each one.
The message from AI leaders is not “stop using AI.” It is that as these systems become more powerful, safety measures, human oversight, and governance must advance with them.
Why AI gets things wrong
AI is powerful, but it is not fool proof. Its output depends on the quality of its data, system design, and the context it receives. Human judgement remains essential.
If the data are inaccurate, outdated or poorly organized, AI can produce an unreliable answer with great confidence. It may also reproduce biases contained in historical data.
Generative AI has another key weakness. It can produce information that sounds plausible but is false. It may generate an incorrect statistic, invent a source, or provide a misleading explanation. This phenomenon, commonly called an AI “hallucination,” can be dangerous when such an answer is accepted without verification.
AI can also fail because it lacks important context. A sales forecasting system may recommend increasing production after analyzing years of sales data. But if a major customer cancelled an order yesterday and that information was not included, the forecast could be seriously wrong.
The lesson is simple: AI output should never be treated as automatically correct, especially when it informs financial, legal, safety, or employment decisions.
Matters for Bangladesh
Bangladeshi businesses cannot afford to adopt expensive technology because it is trendy. Many companies still struggle with basic data management. Records may be scattered across departments, stored in inconsistent formats, or divided between Bangla and English.
AI cannot fix these weaknesses. Poor data fed into a sophisticated AI system can and will simply produce mistakes faster and with greater confidence. Before investing heavily in AI, businesses should improve the quality, accessibility, security, and governance of their data.
A two-track response
Bangladesh does not need to panic about AI, nor should it rush blindly into it. The right approach is responsible acceleration: Move quickly where AI can improve productivity and competitiveness, but proceed more carefully where it affects people's money, safety, privacy, or livelihoods.
Policy-makers should consider establishing a national AI safety and governance council comprising experts from technology, industry, cybersecurity, law, economics, academia, and government.
Its purpose should not be to slow adoption, but to keep governance in step with expanding AI capabilities. It could identify high-risk applications, establish testing standards, recommend safeguards, and create a system for learning from serious AI-related failures.
Regulation should be risk-based rather than one-size-fits-all. A company using AI to summarize documents should not face the same requirements as a bank using it to assess loans. The greater the potential harm, the stronger the safeguards should be.
Businesses and industrialists should begin with applications where the benefits are clear and the risks manageable, such as document processing, internal research, demand forecasting, quality control, and routine customer service. They should be more cautious before giving AI greater autonomy over decisions involving customers' money, employees' livelihoods, or operational safety.
Humans should remain responsible for consequential decisions. Employees need training to recognize AI's limitations and verify its output. Cybersecurity should likewise be a leadership priority wherever AI systems connect to financial, customer or production systems.
Above all, business leaders should stop asking, “Where can we use AI?” and instead ask, “What problem are we trying to solve, and is AI the safest and most effective way to solve it?”
Adopting AI for its own sake can add cost and complexity without creating real value.
Keeping pace
Bangladesh cannot afford to miss the productivity gains AI offers. Our manufacturers, exporters, banks, and public institutions will increasingly need it to remain competitive. But we should not give increasingly autonomous systems responsibilities that our data, skills, infrastructure, and governance are not yet ready to support.
The goal is not risk-free AI -- that is unrealistic -- but an ecosystem in which risks are identified, assessed, and managed before they become crises. Bangladesh should embrace AI, but with its eyes open.
MM Shahidul Hassan is a distinguished professor at Eastern University, and former Vice Chancellor of East West University, Bangladesh.

item.title: Bangladesh must become indispensable. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
For decades, Bangladesh has asked itself: What do we need from the world to develop ourselves?
Since our independence, we have needed so much support; capital, energy, technology, markets, expertise, and development aid.
As Bangladesh eventually prepares to graduate from least developed country (LDC) status, we also become ever more exposed to increasingly unstable and unpredictable international systems of power and wealth.
It is time we asked ourselves a far more important question: What does the world actually need from Bangladesh?
No country in the 21st century is self-sufficient. A single cellphone has a supply chain with over two thousand steps across 60 countries. Singapore entirely depends on being an intermediary while South Korea, Japan, and Taiwan each import almost everything they need to survive, from food to raw materials.
Bangladesh will continue to depend on foreign markets, investment, and technology -- there is no realistic world where it doesn’t.
There is a difference, however.
Taiwan produces more than 90% of the world’s leading-edge semiconductors, capacity that would take enormous time, capital, and expertise to reproduce.
Even though clothes comprise over 80% of our exports, Bangladesh only produces 6.9% of the global clothing market, a market which is relatively simple to be undercut.
That is the difference between dependence and interdependence.
Recent emergencies have made this painfully clear. Aid, resources, and energy are prioritized not simply to the rich, but to countries indispensable for the global economy.
When wars, energy and trade disruptions, and climatic events hit with ever-increasing frequency; when governments and corporations must choose which relationships to protect and which supply chains to let go off, how many will choose Bangladesh over Egypt, or Morrocco, or even Vietnam?
Goodwill matters, of course, but usefulness is the best insurance. If foreign firms, workers, and governments bear real cost when Bangladesh is disrupted, they have a vested interest in our stability and success because we will have worked to align our interests.
The stronger Bangladesh becomes, the more value we create, the more interests abroad become aligned with our stability and prosperity.
Bangladesh has already shown that we can build systems at scale. In FY2025-26, ready-made garments earned $38.70 billion. We have shown that we can work with an ecosystem of factory-workers, managers, compliance, logistics, and finance, with long-term relationships with thousands of international customers.
Bangladesh's garment industry proves that we can build complicated production ecosystems at enormous scale. The challenge is to learn how to reproduce that process of capability-building in other areas.
We don’t need to do everything, but simply to become reliable enough partners to be an integral part of trade networks.
This being said, indispensability doesn’t simply have to be economic. Thinking only economically can become its own trap.
Decades of necessity have also given us an unusual experience in climate adaptation and disaster management. We should ask whether that experience can become useful -- research, technologies, services, and institutional expertise that other countries increasingly need as climate risks spread.
On the reverse, we need to compound all these capabilities. Development will be useless if we don’t grow the country.
Bangladesh’s net FDI rose 39.36% in 2025 to $1.77 billion. That is a victory, but how much of that will remain after 10 years? Are we increasing the capacity of Bangladeshi engineers? Are we acquiring foreign companies and learning from them? Are we building up Bangladeshi ports to export more or better? Or are increasing the momentum of existing structures and making it ever-more difficult to ever do anything different?
One road will lead to compounding wealth, building within 20 years an excess of resources not seen by our people in over 200 years, enriching both the common people and wealthy alike.
The other will lead us to the looming cliff of climatic and economic disaster which will spare neither our workers, nor our factory owners.
All it takes to pick the right options is to study the problem thoughtfully, bring the appropriate experts from wherever they may be in the world for us to learn from, and to think on the timescale of a decade rather than a quarter.
Becoming “indispensable” doesn’t mean to produce something which degrades our unique value such as “being the cheapest,” nor even something which reduces us to a single element such as “being the most advanced.”
It means to be so fully integrated in a wider system that the system cannot work without us -- not politically, not economically, not culturally.
It means being reliable, taking on responsibility, and compounding our existing advantages to build new ones.
It means believing that we can contribute in our own way something of immense value to others, while at the same time as being interdependent with what they produce.
We already have frameworks with which to work; with Nepal, Bhutan, Southeast Asia, East Asia. But to do so, we need to grow to our potential.
Bangladesh will always need partners. The objective should be to become the kind of partner whose absence creates a problem.
Jean-Salman Marre is a General Manager, Strategy at Friendship NGO.

item.description: THERE has just been yet another surge in fuel prices, the second in the seven-month tenure of the government. Statistics show a staggering 30–40 per cent cumulative increase in prices of various fuels since 2026 began. Energy is the lifeblood of any nation’s economy and the primary driver of its people’s daily lives. Consequently, the devastating shockwaves this massive price hike will send through the economy, the potential inflationary pressure, the cost of living and the political...

item.title: Educated women, unused potential. [ newagebd ]
item.description: THERE is a particular kind of waste that does not appear in economic statistics. It has no smoke, no discarded machinery and no empty warehouse. It happens quietly when an educated woman completes university, acquires skills, perhaps learns another language, develops professional ambitions and then disappears from the labour market. Her education remains with her, but the economy never gets to use it...

item.title: The cost of coastal energy. [ newagebd ]
item.description: ALONG the southern coast, a critical development question is emerging: how can a climate-vulnerable nation expand energy and industrial infrastructure while protecting the ecosystems that sustain millions of people? Rivers, estuaries and coastal waters of Patuakhali, Barguna and neighbouring districts are not merely environmental resources, they are also economic lifelines supporting fisheries, agriculture, transportation and local livelihoods...
